title: What the future of restaurant phone ordering looks like
seoTitle: Future of restaurant phone ordering | ROAL
description: See what may change in restaurant phone ordering, from AI phone hosts to forwarding, pickup calls, and the next steps for small teams.
question: What is the future of restaurant phone ordering for a small restaurant like mine?
answer: Restaurant phone ordering is moving toward AI phone hosts that answer calls, take pickup and delivery orders, and handle common questions without making guests wait on hold. The practical change for owners is simpler: more calls can be captured during rushes, while staff keep control of payments, tricky questions, and special situations.
summary: You’ll know which phone ordering changes matter most and what to set up in your restaurant now.
intro:
Restaurant phone ordering is heading toward a mix of automation and human backup. The phone will still matter, but more restaurants will use an AI phone host to answer routine calls, take orders, and send clean tickets to the kitchen.

For an independent shop, the big shift is not fancy tech. It is fewer missed calls, less pressure on the counter team, and a faster way to handle pickup and delivery orders when the line gets busy.

sections.h2: What will change first in restaurant phone ordering?
sections.body:
The first change is simple: more routine calls will be handled by a phone host instead of interrupting staff. That means pickup orders, basic menu questions, hours, address, parking, and order status can be handled in the same call flow.

For owners, the practical win is less bouncing between the register, the oven, and the ringing phone. A guest can call and hear: "I can take your order, answer menu questions, or connect you with the team if you need something special." That kind of script is built for a pizza shop, deli, or takeout counter.

A useful way to think about it:
- Staff stay focused on food and guests in the store.
- The phone host handles routine phone traffic.
- Tricky calls still go to a person.
- The kitchen gets a clean ticket instead of a handwritten note.

ROAL follows that model. It answers the restaurant's phone, takes pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also speaks the caller's language and passes along allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering requests, and manager requests with a summary.

sections.h2: How will owners set it up without losing control?
sections.body:
The future is not about replacing the restaurant number. It is about routing calls more intelligently. In a normal setup, the owner keeps the existing number and forwards it to the AI phone host, either for all calls or only when the line is busy or unanswered.

That matters because owners can turn forwarding off any time. The phone number stays theirs. That is a much easier step for a busy manager than changing the published number on every menu, flyer, and Google listing.

A simple setup checklist looks like this:
1. Paste the restaurant website, Google Maps link, or "Name, City" into /try.
2. Let the host read the menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages or upload a menu.
3. Test-call it in the browser.
4. Claim the host and forward the restaurant number.
5. Choose a voice and name.
6. Review any unanswered questions in the inbox.

If you want a quick reference for your phone system, use [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes). Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your provider and test with a call. For many owners, that one setup step is the difference between "the phone is ringing again" and "the phone is handled."

sections.h2: What happens to labor costs and order costs?
sections.body:
Restaurant owners usually compare the future of phone ordering against three options: delivery apps, monthly AI phone tools, and human answering help. The numbers matter because the phone is not just a service problem. It is a margin problem.

Here is a simple example you can swap for your own:

| Option | Typical cost pattern | What to plug in |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery apps | Often 15-30% commission per order | Your average check |
| Monthly AI phone tools | Fixed fee, often about $79-$599 per location | Monthly bill whether calls come in or not |
| Human answering services | Usually per minute or per call | Call volume and average call length |
| ROAL | $0.90 per completed phone order | Confirmed orders only |

Say your average phone order is $28. At $0.90 per completed order, the phone fee is easy to understand because you can multiply your own order count by your own order total, then compare that against your current method. If you want to run the math, use [the AI phone host cost calculator](/tools/phone-host-cost-calculator) and plug in your own order count.

A future-focused restaurant usually wants two things at once: lower fixed cost and less staff interruption. That is why many owners are looking closely at [pay per order vs monthly AI phone plans](/compare/monthly-ai-phone-plans). The right choice depends on how often your phone rings, how often staff can answer, and how much of that traffic is really just routine ordering.

sections.h2: How will the kitchen side work when calls get busier?
sections.body:
The kitchen side of phone ordering is where the future gets practical. A call should not end with a scrambled note or a half-heard order. It should end with a ticket your team can read quickly.

A clean phone workflow usually includes:
- Items, sizes, modifiers, and notes.
- The caller's name and phone number.
- A quoted ready time.
- Confirmation of the order back to the caller.
- A live ticket that lands on the kitchen screen.

For example, the host might say: "Just to confirm, that is one large pepperoni, one order of wings well done, and no onions on the salad. Your order will be ready in 20 minutes." That kind of repetition helps prevent mistakes.

This is also where guardrails matter. The host should not offer items marked sold out. It should not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it. That keeps the phone simple and keeps staff in control of the parts that need a person.

If you are comparing tools, the useful question is not "Can it answer?" It is "Can it take the order the way my team needs it written?"

sections.h2: What should happen when the phone host does not know the answer?
sections.body:
No phone host knows everything on day one, and that is normal. The important part is what happens next. The best workflow is to send unknown questions to an inbox so the owner can answer once and the host remembers it from then on.

That creates a better setup for the next caller. It also keeps staff from repeating the same answer all day. A good ownership habit is to review those questions after service, not during a rush.

A practical handling list:
1. Let the host answer hours, address, menu, parking, and basic order questions.
2. Send allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering, and manager requests to staff.
3. Review the inbox once a day.
4. Add the answer to the menu, FAQs, or hours if it keeps coming up.
5. Test the next call to make sure the host now knows it.

This is one area where ROAL is built to fit a real restaurant day. It hands off tricky calls with a summary, and it keeps an inbox for questions it could not answer. If you want more context on that flow, see [when the AI doesn't know the answer](/blog/ai-phone-host-unanswered-questions).

sections.h2: What should an owner do now to be ready for the next few years?
sections.body:
The future of restaurant phone ordering is not a far-off idea. It is a series of small decisions you can make now: cleaner menu data, better call routing, clearer hours, and a phone workflow that protects your team during rushes.

Here is a simple readiness checklist for a pizza shop, deli, or family restaurant:
- Your menu is current and readable from public pages or an upload.
- Your hours and address are correct everywhere callers look.
- Your team knows which calls should stay with staff.
- Your forwarding setup is tested.
- Your kitchen screen can handle live tickets.
- Your phone greeting sounds like your restaurant, not a machine.

If you want to try the setup without a big project, [build a free test host](/try) from your website and test-call it in the browser. ROAL was built by Venkata Vamsi in Jersey City, NJ, and it works for any US restaurant, but the bigger point is simple: the next phase of phone ordering will reward restaurants that make ordering easier without adding more work for the counter.

Owners who get ahead of this will spend less time fighting the phone and more time running the room, the kitchen, and the food quality.

takeaways: Phone ordering is moving toward routine calls handled by an AI phone host and tricky calls routed to staff.
The biggest gains come from cleaner tickets, faster call handling, and less interruption during rushes.
Keep your restaurant number and forward calls only when it helps your team.
Compare your current costs against per-order, per-minute, and monthly pricing before you switch.

faq.q: Will restaurant phone ordering still matter if customers use apps more?
faq.a: Yes. Many guests still call when they want pickup, have menu questions, need quick changes, or want to talk to the restaurant directly. Phone ordering is especially useful for local regulars and for orders that need a human-style conversation.

faq.q: Can an AI phone host take the order and send it to the kitchen?
faq.a: Yes. ROAL answers the phone, takes pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, confirms the details back to the caller, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also collects the caller's name and phone number.

faq.q: Should I forward all calls to an AI phone host or only some of them?
faq.a: Either can work. Many owners start with all calls, while others forward only busy or unanswered calls. The safest approach is to test both and keep the setup that protects service during rushes without making the phone feel disconnected.

faq.q: What should an AI phone host not handle?
faq.a: It should not take card numbers over the phone, and it should pass along allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering requests, and manager requests to staff. That keeps payment and sensitive situations in the hands of your team.
